summary.value: This paper proposes a simple variant of beam search in which the beam size grows monotonically at each node with the entropy of the model. The paper provides theoretical analyses using a model of risk of missing the argmax, as well as some analysis of using their method when one has only sampling ability from an API. The paper provides compute-matched comparisons with beam search, and non-compute-matched comparisons with sampling algorithms like top-p. Evaluations are run on humaneval, gsm8k, and math500. The authors also run experiments in a simulated API setting and run a synthetic noise-dependence study.

strengths.value: This paper provides a really nice simple algorithm for adaptively spending more compute while generating from language models. I think it’s well-motivated, clearly described, and while I don’t draw too much insight from the theory because it rests on premises I don’t think really hold, I still found the theoretical discussion thought-provoking, so I consider the theory a win overall. If this method is a better use of compute than sampling multiple times from a model with top-p, this would be a great contribution. Unfortunately, we just don’t know if this is the case (see below.)

weaknesses.value:
The summary here is that I really want to like this paper but in order to draw conclusions from it, I need the core experiments to be stronger, in particular by comparing EDEN not just to beam search but to methods in which we use a large p in top-p and sample multiple times from a model and take the best or most likely under the model (which is a standard way to spend more compute on finding good generations under a model.) I also don’t feel like I can conclude too much from the theory (details below,) but I consider this not a huge issue.

I was really hoping that the experiments would include compute-matching between not just EDEN and beam search, but also between EDEN and sampling methods like top-p. Calling methods like top-p (or min-p, or even top-k) “not entropy-adaptive” seems just wrong. Indeed, if one considers sampling multiple times from each model, then they’re all adaptive on entropy. Indeed, by computing multiple full sequence-level samples from each model under each sampling method and then taking the highest-likelihood under that set, all of these methods adaptively explore “more” in expectation from prefixes for which the model being sampled from has high conditional entropy. Computing these most-likely-of-n metrics for sampling is standard, and one can compute-match by matching the expected number of conditional distributions one must compute for each (e.g., num_samples*seq_len for the sampling methods.) On this note, using temperature=0.6 with top-p=0.9 is really really close to greedy decoding in many circumstances, so if you compare in this setting, you should make sure to sample from a wider distribution (e.g., top-p 0.95, temperature=1)

On that note, just a few more models – especially stronger models! – evaluated in Table 1 would be a great use of space to make the experiments stronger. Testing just a single model is not preferable.

The entropy as a proxy for hardness doesn’t make a lot of sense in distributions with desirable – aleatoric – uncertainty, e.g., building a good model of text means generating many things for the prefix “My name is” but this has nothing to do with the computational hardness of the problem. The analysis and lemmas provided in section 3 have the assumption that there’s a single correct candidate, which is not true. Overall I found the analysis nice and thought-provoking, but the setting just doesn’t reflect LM use. The method — “use a larger beam when there’s more uncertainty, independent of the source of that uncertainty” is nice! But the theory provided doesn’t make it better-motivated.

Rarely in modern APIs can we just sample a single token continuation (as opposed to a whole rollout) – rolling out full sequences to estimate each prefix’s entropy would be very expensive – so I’m not sure of the relevance of the closed-model parts of this paper.

The noise model (in embedding space) used for the sensitivity analysis doesn’t make a lot of sense – robustness to embedding noise isn’t necessarily related to real noise distributions – and claims about the connections between paraphrase noise and this don’t make a lot of sense to me because we certainly don’t know what the lipschitz constants of deep networks are (especially with layer norm), and even then small changes in the tokens provided can lead to hard-to-characterize changes in the output distribution.

questions.value:
Notes
- Around 170, it’s odd to have the notion of the entropy of the conditional distribution for a prefix y_{1:t} have the next word y_{t+1} – the entropy (as in the definition you give) does not depend on the real next word y_{t+1}.
- It’s not the case that the highest-probability sequences under a model are the highest-quality – e.g., they assign very high probability to repetitive strings. It would be nice to briefly discuss the conditions under which we do want to maximize probability. The heuristics in top-p seem useful in part because they seem to avoid issues that come up when we try to find the argmax in a high-entropy setting with LLMs (I realize finding the argmax is an intuitive thing to want to do, but indeed it seems like not what we want to do even if we could in mondern times.)
- How is temperature=0.6 default? Where is the default set? I guess I'm saying I don't think most papers use temp=0.6.
- Not required, but it would be nice to cite and briefly discuss Optimal Beam Search for Machine Translation (Rush et al., 2013) in your discussion of your beam pruning strategy.
- I think the delta-greedy row in Table 1 is odd – why are you showing the difference to the cheap greedy method, not the compute-matched Beam search baseline?

Thank you to the reviewers for the kind words and useful suggestions. Below we provide a summary of the consistent positive themes in the reviews and the key changes made to the paper.

We are particularly grateful that the reviewers highlighted the novelty, clarity, and sound theoretical foundation of the proposed approach EDEN. Reviewer xL45 described EDEN as “a really nice idea” that is “thoroughly justified”; reviewer rgbd called it “well-motivated,” “clearly described,” and “a really nice simple algorithm”; reviewer s9ME emphasized the interesting nature of the approach and the fact that it requires minimal hyperparameter tuning; and reviewer friN noted that the method is both clear and novel. We appreciate this strong consensus that the core contribution is valuable, intuitive, and technically well-supported.

We hope during the rebuttal we have successfully addressed the remaining questions and concerns raised during the discussion period. In particular, the paper has been strengthened with the following additions:
- **Stronger statistical testing**: We have now performed statistical significance tests on the resulting Friedman ranks, showing statistically significant difference $p=0.013$ among the methods, and paired this with a Bayesian Hierarchical post-hoc analysis demonstrating EDEN significantly outperforms the comparison approaches (with a 75% posterior probability of being the best method overall). The outcome of this statistical analysis is visible in Table 1 and Figure 3 of the updated manuscript.

- **Additional comparisons** We added direct comparisons to best-of-n and majority voting, two important baselines suggested by reviewers, to Table 1 of the updated manuscript. EDEN outperforms both methods across all evaluated datasets.

- **Additional experimental results**: We now include evaluations on a 7B Mistral model with longer-context generation. Combined with the existing appendix results on Gemma and Granite, this shows that EDEN consistently outperforms the baselines across diverse model sizes, families, and generation lengths.

- **Clarity around scorer**: We have made it clear that MAP is not the only scorer possible, detailing the minimum conditions which must be met in Appendix E.4, and providing additional experimental results on an *external reward model* in Appendix B.2, where the reward model helps improve the resulting generations by controlling the decoding process towards the desirable paths.

- **Asymptotic complexity** We provided a more in-depth breakdown of the cost of EDEN and the comparison  approaches in Appendix C.1, showing the speedup occurs in the average case time complexity. 

We thank the reviewers again for their thoughtful insights, which have helped strengthen the manuscript and better motivate the proposed approach. We believe the extended experimentation, paired with the existing theoretical analysis, provides a clearer and more compelling case for EDEN’s contribution to adaptive decoding as a result.

summary.value: Reviewers broadly agree that EDEN presents a clear and intuitive idea: adaptively allocating search width based on token-level entropy to approximate argmax decoding more efficiently than fixed-width beam search. The paper is seen as technically thoughtful, with a nontrivial theoretical analysis and an appealing entropy-as-uncertainty interpretation, but initially weakened by limited baselines, small model sizes, and insufficient statistical and efficiency evidence. The rebuttal substantially strengthens the empirical case by adding majority voting and best-of-n baselines, statistical significance testing, additional model families and sizes (including 7B), external scorer integration, and clearer theoretical and practical clarifications. Remaining disagreements are mostly about positioning and scope, especially whether EDEN should be framed primarily as an efficiency improvement over beam search rather than a general alternative to sampling, and whether entropy-based theory fully reflects real-world LLM uncertainty.

summary.value: The paper introduces a new decoding strategy, EDEN, which is an adaptive form of mode-seeking search. At each decoding step, the number of expansions for each candidate is determined by the entropy of the logits distribution (and a fixed maximum width), with higher entropy completions being expanded to more candidates and lower entropy completions being expanded to less candidates. EDEN outperforms beam search in 1B-3B models with substantially less candidates expanded.

strengths.value:
S1. I think this is a really nice idea-- it's intuitive and thoroughly justified in the text, and clearly reduces the number of expansions dramatically with improved output quality (e.g. in Figure 3).

S2. The paper has some thoughtful treatment of settings where the entropy distribution is modified by some other decoding strategy, justifying its claim that it can be used in conjunction with temperature or truncation based decoding strategies.

S3. The paper makes an intriguing claim that the method could still work on a model where the logit distribution is not available, such as for closed-source models. I like the framing of presenting Llama results with and without this closed source assumption to compare the performance degradation, although I also have feedback on this section in W3 below.

weaknesses.value:
W1. Some statistical testing should be performed on all results, especially since many of the values in Table 1 are quite close between beam search and EDEN. Bootstrapped confidence intervals would be helpful here. 

W2. I am not convinced by the argument about efficiency starting on line 351. The paper acknowledges in the limitations that there's an additional time penalty for looking at entropy, and heterogenous branching may be harder to balance. The time is the real concern to me-- can you graph wall clock time of beam search vs EDEN vs sampling? It's okay if EDEN isn't the fastest, but this is the real tradeoff, not the number of expanded paths. 

W3. While I'm sympathetic to the expense of using large or API-based models, I think if you are proposing a decoding strategy, you must provide some evidence of its behavior at a more typical scale. This doesn't have to be massive models, and this doesn't need to be every experiment, but we know that decoding methods behave differently when the base model has different capabilities (e.g. beam search outperforming sampling by this much is a bit of an artifact of only evaluating on small models). I'd really like to see two things:
* Some experiments comparing sampling to beam search to EDEN on a 7-8B model; for inference at half precision, this should likely fit on a 16GB GPU. 
* Lower priority than the above, but I think the closed source LLMs argument is really interesting and would be *far* more compelling if you could also demonstrate on a small scale on a closed source model. OpenAI's current cheapest model (gpt-4.1-nano) is $0.10 per 1M input/\$0.40 per 1M output tokens. The simulation of the black-box model in Figure 7 is using 100 random examples from GSM-8k; if you use 1000 tokens per example (600 input + up to 400 output), that would cost ~\$0.03 to run per decoding method! That can be halved if you run batch requests.

W4. More diverse benchmarks would be nice, but that's the most minor of my critiques by far.

In general I'm actually quite positive about this idea, although there are a number of clarifications or additional pieces of evidence I'd really like to see. I'm happy to revise my score after discussion if these concerns are addressed. 

Q1. While I'm generally convinced by your continuity assumption argument, I don't follow the argument in lines 836-837. Why is normalized log-likelihood bounded (other than being trivially bounded above by 0)? Why mention temperature scaling as an example here, especially since most experiments in the paper are run without it?

Q2. Can you provide benchmarking of the efficiency of the method in some metrics other than number of paths expanded? Wall clock time is the one I'd most like to see, though maximum VRAM allocation would also be interesting. 

Q3. How does EDEN scale to 7B models?

Q4. Does the closed source performance translate to improvements on these tasks for an actual closed-source model? 

Q5. Can you discuss how the intuition of EDEN relates to methods like locally typical decoding, which use entropy at each step as well but instead treat it as a measure of information content? 

Other comments/typo feedback (not contributors to the score):
- There are already plenty of entropy-informed decoding methods, so the name is quite vague (and the acronym is pretty contrived). Why not something a bit more descriptive, maybe "Entropy-Dependent ExpansioN"?

- line 854: "preffered" -> "preferred"

And for the questions

### Questions

**Q1:** This is a good question and a very subtle point. The intuition is that temperature serves as a form of regularisation, which makes the output distribution smoother, and thus, helps the Lipschitz regularity assumption.

More formally, the per-step “reward’’ is 
$$r_t = \log P_\mathcal{T}(x_{t+1}\mid x_{1:t}) = \frac{1}{\mathcal{T}} z_{x_{t+1}} - \log \sum_j e^{z_j / \mathcal{T}},$$
where $z$ are the model logits and $\mathcal{T}$ is the temperature. Since logits are finite, both terms are bounded, implying  $r_t \in [-\log V, 0]$ in the uniform limit. In practice, these bounds are typically much tighter, and increasing $\mathcal{T}$ further contracts the logit range by $\frac{1}{\mathcal{T}}$, and consequently makes $r_t$ *Lipschitz* with constant proportional to $\frac{1}{\mathcal{T}}$.  

As $\mathcal{T} \to \infty$, the distribution approaches uniformity, so $r_t \to -\log V$; in this limit, the predictive distribution is completely smooth and the Lipschitz regularity condition holds trivially. However, additionally, since both the softmax and log-likelihood mappings are smooth and bounded for any such temperature, this holds for $\mathcal{T} > 0$. Thus, temperature scaling is cited as an illustrative mechanism ensuring that per-step log-likelihoods remain bounded and smooth, supporting the *Lipschitz regularity assumption*, though the argument continues to hold for $\mathcal{T} = 1$ as well.

**Q2, Q3, Q4**: See W2 and W3 above.

**Q5**: Locally typical decoding adjusts sampling probabilities based on deviation from the model’s conditional entropy, maintaining each token’s information content near its expected value to produce linguistically “normal” and diverse text. In contrast, EDEN interprets entropy as a measure of epistemic uncertainty, allocating computational effort adaptively by expanding more branches in high-entropy regions. 

Thus, the two methods are complementary: locally typical decoding regulates informational diversity, while EDEN regulates search effort. The locally typical decoding work may suggest alternate scoring criteria to use within the proposed approach, e.g., by adding a penalty to the per-step reward based on deviations from the information content (i.e., $\rho$ in Appendix E.4), instead of relying only on cumulative log prob if the goal is more linguistically *normal* text.

**Other comments**: We have made most of these modifications in the text, e.g., adding arrows to the tables, specifying the llama version, correcting stylisation, and adding the relevant HARP reference.

Thank you again for the useful comments and questions! If you have any additional comments or follow ups, we will be glad to address them during the rebuttal.

Thank you very much for the thorough review and comments! Due to character limits, we will focus on the weaknesses below, and on the questions in a follow-up comment.

### Weaknesses

**W1**: We have now added extensive statistical testing, detailed in the comment below, and shown in Figure 3 and Table 1 in the updated manuscript, demonstrating that EDEN convincingly outperforms all comparisons. Additionally,  as we have now ran many experiments across different models (Llama, Gemma, Granite, see Appendix B), different sizes (1B, 2B, 3B, 7B), and different scenarios (Different $T$, $\lambda$, quantization), the consistency of these results, with EDEN consistently achieving the highest rank across the settings, helps further strengthen the robustness claims. With these many different runs, the resulting ranks and results are very stable, with EDEN always maintaining the top overall spot.

**W2**: We have now added to the appendix (Appendix C.1) a breakdown of the big-O costs of the various approaches in terms of time (worst and average), memory usage, and GPU suitability, to give a more generic implementation agnostic representation. Included here for your reference:

| Method | Time (Worst) | Time (Avg.) | Memory | GPU Suit. | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Greedy | O(TC) | O(TC) | O(TK) | Excellent | Fastest baseline; batch=1. |
| Top-k/Top-p | O(TC) | O(TC) | O(TK) | Excellent | Same cost as greedy; high throughput. |
| Best-of-n | O(nTC) | O(nTC) | O(TK)...O(nTK) | High | Perfect batching; high throughput. |
| Majority Vote | O(nTC) | O(nTC) | O(TK)...O(nTK) | High | Same as best-of-n; voting negligible. |
| Beam Search (b) | O(bTC) | O(bTC) | O(bTK) | Fair | Homogeneous branches. |
| **EDEN** | O($B_\text{max}$TC) | O((∑ₜᴛ Bₜ)C) | O($B_\text{max}$TK) | Fair | Heterogeneous branches; small entropy overhead |

where T = generation length, C = per-token forward cost, b = beam width, n = number of samples, K = the per-token memory cost,  and $B_\text{max}$ = EDEN's maximum branching factor.

EDEN reduces the average time case of beam search due to the adaptive allocation. In terms of GPU compatibility, at worst, EDEN would be the same as beam search (as we could mask the beams not included in $B_t$), but the significantly fewer expansions offer a promising speedup. We provide a breakdown of the wall-clock overhead of computing entropy (which is constant in the vocab size $|\mathcal{V}|$) versus a forward pass (which is quadratic in the token length $T$) in Appendix C, Figure 7, to show that this is a very negligible calculation for the amount of expansion savings particularly as $T$ grows. 

We stress that the approach is not currently optimized for the HuggingFace library (instead following our Algorithm 1), so the wall-clock time of the overall method would be comparing implementation details rather than the underlying method, but we hope the above asymptotic analysis is useful.

Additionally, we feel the number of expansions is still an important and relevant criterion, for example, if needing to pay for completions (e.g., through a provider), this becomes crucial, and additionally, its comparable across different implementations/optimizations. So through combining the expansion counts, the asymptotic analysis, and quality/accuracy results, we get a good view of the tradeoffs among the approaches.

|-----------|-------|
| Greedy    | 37%   |
| Min-p     | 42%   |
| Top-p     | 37%   |
| Top-k     | 39%   |
| Beam      | 46%   |
| EDEN      | **47%**   |

**Questions**: Entropy is computed *after* these have been applied. So for example, in the closed source setting, the entropy is just over the returned top-$k$, while in the general setting, it's over the full output distribution (and after temperature scaling).


Thank you again for the useful suggestions, we believe these have substantially strengthed the emperical support. If you have further concerns or questions we would be glad to further address these.

summary.value:
This work proposes a novel search algorithm called EDEN. The core idea is to perform argmax decoding by estimating and branching factor at each search step using the entropy of the token level distribution. Authors described all the math behind proving the correctness of their algorithm that aligns with a clear logic: higher entropy needs wider search / larger branching. Then authors show how one can use API models as well to approximate EDEN decoding even without having the access to token-level sampling control.
Authors perform experiments over a wide range of tasks using public benchmarks, and compared their method with other search and sampling algorithms. They showed how their approach outperform baselines they chose to report using a few different underlying models for generation.

strengths.value: * the method sounds clear and contribute with a novel technique. I will focus more on the discussion of why I believe it could be presented better in the next section.

weaknesses.value:
I like the proposed idea of branching, while i believe it might have been applied / tested under a much more convincing experimental design and baselines.
First is the choice of baseline generation methods. We have to compare this to aggregation based decoding such as majority voting and related methods, since they can be seen as performing argmax decoding too (see the original self-consistency decoding paper). 
Second, lots of prior work suggest that model log score is not the best choice for choosing / ranking answers with LLMs. This is where the best test-time scaling methods use external scoring models to choose the final answer. Looks like eden might be combined with step-level score models etc., but it was not discussed much in the paper.
Third, stronger and newer LLMs have to be tested here. There are much stronger and smaller LLMs than llama3.2 3b out there that can generate multiple thousands tokens of reasoning. This is where branching can be so helpful! Current numbers with 400 generated tokens are way too limited to be convincing.

comment.value:
Thank you very much for the review and comments!

**Novelty and Related work**: As discussed in Section 2, most adaptive-width approaches in prior work (including Lin et al., now added) make branching decisions using relatively ad-hoc rules. In contrast, our use of entropy as the branching signal is both principled and theoretically justified: we show that entropy directly governs the statistical hardness of next-token selection and derive a monotone allocation rule with guarantees (Theorem 3.3). While the intuition of “expanding more when uncertain” is not new in general search, to our knowledge, no previous decoding method uses entropy with formal analysis to determine beam width.

Regarding the recency of many references: we focused deliberately on LLM decoding because modern LLMs provide *rich and highly informative* next-token distributions $P(y_{t+1} \mid x, \mathbf{y}_{1:t})$ at every step. These distributions already encode meaningful structure that can be used directly to guide search, removing the need to learn such a distribution. In contrast, earlier models and classical search methods (e.g., MCTS) typically had to estimate or construct such distributions through repeated sampling or rollouts. Because our method relies fundamentally on leveraging the native informativeness of LLM output distributions, the most relevant prior work occurs in the recent LLM setting.  We agree that earlier search work is relevant for context, and have now added references to key older work such as Optimal Beam Search (2013), which supports our branch-and-bound pruning, as well as Diverse Beam Search (2016, 2018), whose objective could be viewed as an alternative scoring function under EDEN. We also note that entropy and relative entropy have classical uses in language model pruning and control (e.g., early LM pruning work such as "Entropy-based Pruning of Backoff Language Models", A. Stolcke, 2000), but these operate in a different regime and were therefore excluded to keep the related work focused on the closest methods.


**Lipschitz assumption empirical validation**:  We have added an empirical example in Appendix E.3 demonstrating that this assumption holds for the base Llama model. There, we quantify the local Lipschitz behavior of continuation values under small perturbations to the model’s next-token distribution.

Across 100 sampled prompts from GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, and SciBench, we estimate both a global least-squares Lipschitz constant ($\approx 0.04$) and a 95th-percentile local constant ($\approx 1.5$). These small values indicate that continuation values are insensitive to modest perturbations of the next-token distribution, providing empirical support for the assumption.


To measure this, we
- Sample multiple continuations from the base embeddings
- Sample multiple continuations from perturbed embeddings
- Measure the induced total-variation shift in the next-token distribution, and
- Record the resulting change in continuation log-likelihood.

Plotting $|\Delta V|$ versus $\mathrm{TV}(P,\tilde P)$ across many perturbations shows that the resulting (local) Lipschitz constants are very small, demonstrating empirically that the Lipschitz continuity assumption holds in our setting.


**MAP vs. Sampling**: We agree that no approach (MAP or sampling) is universally superior, but felt it was important to include these comparisons since EDEN’s goal is a decoding framework, not exclusively a beam-search optimization, it is important to evaluate it against the full set of commonly used decoding strategies, including sampling. Additionally, per other reviewer suggestions, we have now added additional comparisons to majority voting and best-of-$n$ to Table 1 to give a broader comparison. 

Additionally, EDEN is compatible with various scorers (as discussed in the new Appendix E.4), which may help overcome some of the limitations you have mentioned of MAP. Although our experiments use a MAP-style score, any scorer satisfying the outlined assumptions can be plugged into EDEN to dynamically allocate compute based on entropy. For example, Appendix B.2 features a scorer augmented by an external reward model to show the flexibility. 

Thank you again for the review and discussions! We hope the above addresses any of your remaining concerns.

summary.value: The authors propose an adaptive beam search strategy which adjust the amount of branching based on the entropy of the next-token distribution. They provide a theoretical analysis that justifies their design and gives guarantees about the optimality of their method. Finally, they show that in the restricted API setting, the method continues to work because top-k probabilities allow for robust estimation of next-token distribution entropy even for modest k.

strengths.value: The subject matter is interesting, the method makes sense, the theoretical analysis seems reasonable. I like that the method requires minimal hyperparameter tuning (basically, just need to set the maximum budget).

weaknesses.value:
I am concerned about the novelty of the method. A cursory search by ChatGPT surfaced Lin et al. (2018) who propose a method that adapts the beam search width based on the model's probability assigned to the search paths. Their method appears to be less theoretically justified and does not explicitly use entropy, but the kernel of the idea is there: search less when the model is confident, search more when it is unsure. I noticed that the related work section cites no papers prior to 2024, which is a red flag to me, since beam search and other decoding methods predate this by a wide margin. What other methods exist that adjust beam width based on entropy (or proxies of entropy)?

The Lipschitz assumption strikes me as something that can be empirically supported. Is there a reason that you do not? It would make your choice much more justified if you could show that the assumption holds generally for some specific language models.

As far as I can tell, you do not seem to address one of the major shortcomings of MAP decoding approximations like beam search, namely that the most likely sequence is not necessarily natural (Stahlberg et al. 2018). While this is not specific to your method, (it afflicts beam search as well) it might be misleading to claim that your method trumps sampling methods like top-k/p. In the specific task of factual question answering, math, and coding tasks, MAP is known to do well, but in more open-ended tasks and creative tasks, sampling methods often win. 

Upon further consideration, your results showing that your method beats sampling methods (like top-p/k) are nothing new, these same results would manifest themselves were you to just use beam search. The advantage of your method over existing methods, as I understand it, is that it allows for a more *efficient* beam search, with the same expected outcome of beam search with a correspondingly large width budget. Therefore, I would recommend that you frame your work solely around an efficiency comparison with beam search. I think the comparisons with sampling methods are out of scope, perhaps irrelevant, unless you have something new to add to conversation about MAP vs. sampling.

[1] Lin, Yu-Hsiang et al. “Adaptive Beam Search in Sequence-to-Sequence Models.” (2018).

[2] Stahlberg, Felix and Bill Byrne. “On NMT Search Errors and Model Errors: Cat Got Your Tongue?” ArXiv abs/1908.10090 (2019): n. pag.

comment.value:
Thank you for the positive comments and useful feedback! Due to character limits, we will reply to the weaknesses below and the questions separately.

**Experiments**: We added comparisons to best-of-n and majority voting (with n = max beam size for $\approx$ expansion-matched comparisons), with the suggested parameters of top-p=0.95 and temperature=1 to Table 1. While both achieve good results, EDEN still outperforms these methods on all four datasets, remaining in the top overall ranked position. 

**Models**: We have evaluated additional models (including Gemma and Granite) in Appendix B, and early added results on Mistral in Appendix B.1.1. 

**Entropy adaptive**: This is a good point that repeated stochastic rollouts (with $\mathcal{T}$>0) will begin to approximate entropy adaptive sampling in *expectation*, and is related to the point below about full rollouts. However, the crucial distinction here is “Adaptive in expectation” vs “Adaptive allocation”.

While we agree that sampling multiple times leads to a similar expectation, this does not adaptively allocate compute per step, instead having fixed compute $m/t$ per step. The distinction is important: increasing stochastic exploration (e.g., with more full-sequence samples) alters output variance but keeps the per-step compute fixed, while entropy-adaptive allocation changes the per-step compute itself. The convex optimization / KKT solution in Appendix E.2, and the Monte Carlo plot in Figure 2, demonstrate that the latter strictly dominates the former in terms of the number of samples required whenever stepwise entropies differ.

**Token-level continuation and Full rollouts**: EDEN is designed to operate at various node-level continuations. Here, we have explored tokens as nodes, but the formed tree could also be at a higher level, e.g., at the tool call level, or a sequence level. This is something we have begun exploring (sequence level extensions) as future work, e.g., by averaging the entropy of nodes through multiple rollouts, and only performing continuations from high entropy points. We feel this deserves a full analysis for future work. With this extension, compatibility with closed-source APIs becomes more realistic, e.g., estimating entropy based on repeated output samples not necessarily just at the token level.

**Single output**: While we have considered a single output under most probable scoring, as EDEN builds a decoding tree, we do have multiple potential outputs (e.g., each completed path)! For instance, with the "my name is" example, various outcomes would be different branches (constrained by the beam width) in the tree. If each name is equally likely, they will continue to be expanded (up to the maximum beam width). At the end, if there are multiple potential paths (with similar likelihoods), all could be returned instead of just a single path. However, in the case of one continuation (e.g., one name) being more likely, this continuation would be followed unless considering alternate scorers explicitly (as discussed below).

**Aleatoric uncertainty**: We highlight in Appendix F: Limitations (Confidence) that model entropy does not always reflect task difficulty, and maximum-likelihood is not always the best scorer to use.

However, importantly, EDEN does not necessarily rely only on using just this maximum likelihood scorer with per-step reward $r_t(i) = \log p_i$. Therefore, we have relaxed this in Appendix E.4, which shows that our analysis extends to scorers under the following assumptions:
- Additive, bounded per-step rewards $r_t$,
- Distributional Lipschitz continuity,
- Monotone entropy–gap structure (which can be maintained by bounded log-likelihood perturbations),  
- Sub-Gaussian rollout concentration (a consequence of bounded rewards).

This includes, for example, likelihood perturbed by uncertainty-aware terms, allowing one to move away from just “maximum likelihood = correct”. For example, the likelihood reward could be perturbed with an explicit uncertainty-aware term (as in "Uncertainty Estimation for Safety-critical Scene Segmentation via Fine-grained Reward Maximization" (2023), or "Uncertainty-aware Reward Model: Teaching Reward Models to Know What is Unknown" (2024). Formally, one may use a scorer of the form

$$F(y_{1:T}) = F_{\mathrm{LL}}(y_{1:T}) + \lambda R(y_{1:T}), \qquad R(y_{1:T})=\sum_{t=1}^T \rho_t(y_t,x,y_{1:t-1})$$

where $\rho_t$ encodes the desired uncertainty structure (for example, a KL-divergence from a desired output distribution, as per your name example, this could be uniform), ensuring EDEN does not over-allocate compute to intrinsically aleatoric steps while still satisfying the above assumptions.

Thank you again for the comments and suggestions! Please see the comment below for the smaller questions.
